title: Telling Time to the Minute (Grade 3): A Clear, Step-by-Step Guide + Free Quiz
meta_title: Telling Time to the Minute Grade 3 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach telling time to the minute in Grade 3: read the minute hand exactly, minutes past and to, a.m. vs p.m., and elapsed time. Free quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: In Grade 2 a child learns o’clock, half past and quarter past. Grade 3 is where the clock gets honest — every little mark counts, and 3:47 has to mean 3:47. Here is how to teach it without the tears, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Show a Grade 2 child a clock at 3:47 and most will confidently say ‘quarter to four’ and stop there. Show the same clock to a child who has cracked telling time to the minute in Grade 3, and they will tell you it is 3:47 — or, if they are thinking the other way, thirteen minutes to four. That jump, from the nearest quarter to the exact minute, is the whole point of Grade 3 time. It sounds small. In my experience teaching eight-year-olds, it is the single messiest topic of the year, because it asks a child to read two hands that move at completely different speeds and mean completely different things.

The good news: it breaks into a handful of clean ideas. Get them in the right order and the confusion clears up fast.

Start with what each mark on the clock means

Before a child can read 3:47, they have to accept one fact: the small marks between the numbers each stand for one minute. There are 60 of them, five between every pair of numbers. This is the gap between Grade 2 and Grade 3 in a single sentence. In Grade 2 the minute hand only ever landed on 12, 3, 6 or 9. Now it can land anywhere.

I teach it as a two-speed count. First count the numbers in fives — 5, 10, 15, 20 — to get near the minute hand. Then count the leftover little marks in ones. For the minute hand sitting two marks past the 9, you count 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45 to reach the 9, then 46, 47. That is 47 minutes. Slow, yes. But it is the honest method, and speed comes with repetition.

The two hands do two different jobs

The commonest mistake I see is reading the hour hand as if it points at an exact number. At 3:47 the short hand is almost touching the 4 — and children announce ‘4 something’. The rule that fixes this: the hour is whatever number the short hand has most recently passed, never the one it is heading towards. At 3:47 it has passed 3 and not yet reached 4, so it is still 3:47, not 4:47.

  • The short, fat hand tells the hour. Read the number it has already gone past.
  • The long, thin hand tells the minutes. Count in fives, then ones.
  • A red or thin sweeping hand, if the clock has one, is the seconds — ignore it for now.

Minutes past and minutes to

Grade 3 wants children to read a time both ways. Up to and including 30 minutes we usually say minutes past the hour: 3:20 is ‘twenty past three’. After 30 we flip to minutes to the next hour: 3:47 is ‘thirteen minutes to four’, because 47 and 13 make 60.

The ‘to’ direction trips children up because it needs a subtraction. Teach it as counting up to 60: from 47, how many more to reach 60? Thirteen. So it is 13 minutes to the next hour. A child who knows their number bonds to 60 — or can count on — handles this comfortably.

a.m., p.m. and a light touch of 24-hour time

A clock face shows 3:47 twice a day. a.m. is midnight to noon; p.m. is noon to midnight. The anchors worth drilling: 12 a.m. is midnight, 12 p.m. is noon — the two most confused times on the whole clock. I tie them to a child’s own day: 7 a.m. is breakfast, 3 p.m. is home from school, 9 p.m. is bedtime.

Grade 3 only needs a light introduction to 24-hour time — enough to recognise that 3 p.m. is the same moment a train timetable calls 15:00. Do not over-teach it. Add 12 to any afternoon or evening hour and you have the 24-hour version; that is plenty for now.

Elapsed time: how long is it from 3:15 to 3:50?

This is where Grade 3 time earns its keep, because it turns clock-reading into a real-life skill. Elapsed time is simply how long passed between two clock times. From 3:15 to 3:50, both times share the same hour, so you subtract the minutes: 50 − 15 = 35 minutes.

When the times cross an hour, I teach jumping to the next o’clock first. From 3:50 to 4:20: it is 10 minutes from 3:50 to 4:00, then another 20 from 4:00 to 4:20, so 30 minutes altogether. This ‘bridge through the hour’ method beats counting one minute at a time, and it mirrors how adults actually work out how long until a bus arrives.

How the pieces fit together

Clock showsMinutes pastMinutes toSaid aloud
4:055 past 4—Five past four
4:2020 past 4—Twenty past four
4:3030 past 430 to 5Half past four
4:4747 past 413 to 5Thirteen to five
4:5555 past 45 to 5Five to five

One honest caveat from the classroom: a real geared clock is worth more than any app. On a cheap plastic learning clock the hour hand actually creeps as the minutes pass, so at 3:47 it sits almost on the 4 — exactly the tricky case children need to see. A printed clock face where the hour hand always points dead-on lies to them, and they get caught out later.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free, eight-question quiz covering exactly what we have worked through — reading to the minute, minutes past and to, a.m. and p.m., and elapsed time. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for any they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice with real clock faces, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Telling Time Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on reading the clock to the minute, minutes past and to, a.m. and p.m., and elapsed time. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 3 telling time to the minute

questions.q: The minute hand points two little marks past the 9. What minute is it?
questions.explanation: Count in fives to the 9 (45), then two ones more: 46, 47. So it is 47 minutes.

questions.q: The short hand is just before the 4 and the minute hand shows 47. What time is it?
questions.explanation: The hour is the number the short hand has passed. It has passed 3 but not reached 4, so it is 3:47.

questions.q: How do we say 5:20 using 'minutes past'?
questions.explanation: Up to 30 minutes we say minutes past the hour, so 5:20 is twenty past five.

questions.q: What is another way to say 8:50?
questions.explanation: After 30 minutes we count to the next hour. 50 and 10 make 60, so 8:50 is ten to nine.
12 a.m. is midnight and 12 p.m. is noon. These two are the most commonly confused times.

questions.q: A film starts at 3:15 and ends at 3:50. How long is it?
questions.explanation: Both times are in the same hour, so subtract the minutes: 50 minus 15 = 35 minutes.

questions.q: How long is it from 3:50 to 4:20?
questions.explanation: Bridge through the hour: 10 minutes to reach 4:00, then 20 more to 4:20. That is 30 minutes.

questions.q: A train timetable shows 15:00. What time is that on a normal clock?
questions.explanation: For afternoon 24-hour times, subtract 12: 15 minus 12 = 3, so 15:00 is 3 p.m.

faq.q: What time-telling skills should a Grade 3 child master?
faq.a: Reading an analogue clock to the exact minute, saying a time as minutes past and minutes to, telling a.m. from p.m., and working out elapsed time between two clock times. This builds on the o’clock, half and quarter times learned in Grade 2.

faq.q: Why does my child read 3:47 as 4-something?
faq.a: They are reading the hour hand as if it points at the number it is closest to. Teach the rule that the hour is whatever number the short hand has already passed — at 3:47 it has passed 3, so it is still 3, even though it looks nearly at the 4.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to teach minutes to the hour?
faq.a: Count up to 60 rather than subtracting. For 3:47, ask how many more minutes to reach 60: the answer is 13, so it is thirteen minutes to four. Children who know their number bonds find this quick.

faq.q: How should I teach elapsed time across an hour?
faq.a: Bridge through the next o’clock. From 3:50 to 4:20, count 10 minutes up to 4:00, then 20 more to 4:20, giving 30 minutes. It is far more reliable than counting single minutes and matches how we work out waiting times in real life.
